codex-t1-c1.title: Chapter 1 — The Beginning
codex-t1-c1.html:
The port had been rumbling since dawn, an endless ballet of metal cranes and containers hanging in the damp early-morning air. The smell of salt mixed with diesel, a combination Takeshi had grown used to over the years, to the point of barely noticing it anymore. He wore a fluorescent orange vest over a jacket too thin for the cold, thick gloves whose fingertips were starting to wear through, and that closed, almost absent expression he usually kept on during working hours.

His job was to guide the containers from the ground while the cranes moved them from one cargo ship to another, coordinating his gestures with the crackling radio clipped to his shoulder. It was physical, repetitive work, but at least it had the merit of never leaving him too much time to think — something he appreciated without ever quite admitting it to himself.

Around ten o'clock, the break siren rang out across the whole quay, and the workers began to converge on the little prefab hut that served as a break room, wedged between two metal hangars. Takeshi went along with the rest of his crew, pulling off his gloves before pushing the door open, the artificial warmth of the electric heater an immediate contrast with the cold outside.

Two of his coworkers were already settled around the small Formica table, a tired coffee maker sputtering in a corner. Marco, a stocky man in his fifties who had worked the docks longer than anyone could remember, was already rolling out a story about the previous night's soccer match, while Sana, younger, listened with half an ear as she scrolled through something on her phone.

— Ah, Takeshi! Marco called out when he saw him come in. Come tell me I'm right, that penalty was clearly a joke.

Takeshi let out a small, barely audible laugh and headed for the coffee maker to pour himself a coffee in a paper cup slightly split at the rim.

— I didn't watch the game, Marco. You know I stopped following that years ago.

— That's a scandal, Marco muttered, shaking his head, an amused smile on his lips all the same. A young man with no passion for soccer. In my day, that didn't even exist.

Sana finally looked up from her phone, a crooked smile forming on her face.

— Leave him alone, Marco. Not everyone needs to get worked up over eleven guys chasing a ball like dogs after a tennis ball.

— It's a lack of general culture, Marco insisted, but without any real conviction, his attention already drifting back to his own coffee.

Takeshi sat down on one of the slightly wobbly metal chairs, the hot cup between his hands, enjoying these few minutes of relative quiet before he had to go back out into the fine rain that was starting to fall again. He looked out the hut's small window for a moment, watching the cranes slowly resume their movement in the distance, the hanging containers swaying gently against the gray sky.

— You look tired, Sana said suddenly, watching him a little more closely than usual. You okay?

Takeshi gave a slight shrug, his eyes still turned toward the window.

— Yeah, I'm fine. Just slept badly.

— The nightmares again? she asked, more softly this time, without the slightest trace of mockery in her voice.

He hesitated a moment before answering, his fingers tightening slightly around the hot cup.

— Something like that, yeah.

Marco, who had followed the exchange without really wanting to get involved, gently set his mug down on the table.

— Maybe you should see someone about that, kid. It's been going on for years, hasn't it?

— It's nothing, Takeshi said, a little sharper than he meant to, before catching himself. Really. It always passes after a while.

A slightly awkward silence settled for a few seconds, broken only by the crackle of the coffee maker and the dull, distant thud of containers being maneuvered outside. Sana eventually changed the subject, with the quiet tact of someone who knew not to push, and started telling a story about a delivery guy who had nearly dropped an entire crate of electronics the day before.

Takeshi listened, nodded at the right moments, let out a polite smile when it was called for — but his mind stayed anchored somewhere else, somewhere between the blurry memory of a blue fire and that dull tiredness that, lately, never seemed to leave him entirely.

The siren rang again, shriller this time, signaling the end of the break. Marco got up first, grumbling about how time went by too fast, followed by Sana, who slipped her phone into her pocket before giving Takeshi's shoulder a friendly pat on her way past.

— Take care of yourself, okay? she said simply.

Takeshi nodded, drained the last mouthfuls of his lukewarm coffee and got up in turn, pulling his gloves back on before pushing the hut door open onto the cold and the fine rain of the quay. The cranes were already resuming their endless ballet above him, and he went back to work without another word, his radio crackling against his shoulder, his thoughts still hooked, despite himself, on that tiredness he simply couldn't explain anymore.

Night was already falling when Takeshi left the port, his fluorescent vest swapped for a plain jacket, his hands still a little numb from the cold despite his gloves. He walked to the nearest bus stop, waited about ten minutes under a half-broken shelter, then made the usual trip back to his neighborhood, his head resting against the cold window, watching the city lights roll past without really seeing them.

Once home, he took off his shoes, turned on the hallway light and let himself drop onto the couch with a weary sigh. The cat appeared almost immediately, rubbing insistently against his leg, demanding its evening meal. Takeshi got back up, filled its usual bowl, then went back to sit down, his phone in his hand.

He called his mother first, bringing the phone to his ear while absently rubbing the back of his neck with his other hand. It rang twice before a warm voice answered at the other end.

— Takeshi! How nice, his mother said, a note of happy surprise in her voice. How was your day?

— Tiring, as usual, he answered with a slight smile, settling more comfortably against the back of the couch. But I'm fine. What about you, everything okay?

— Oh, you know, same as always here, she said. Your father tried to fix the gutter by himself again, I'll let you imagine how that went.

Takeshi let out a small laugh, a genuine one this time, a quiet warmth settling in him at the sound of that familiar voice.

— He'll never change.

— No, never, she agreed with amused tenderness. And you, are you at least eating properly? You're not working too much?

— I'm eating fine, Mom, don't worry, he said, his tone a little softer than usual. I've got it handled.

They traded a few more bits of unimportant news — the garden, a neighbor, a cousin who had just had a baby — the conversation drifting easily from one topic to the next, as it always did between them. After about ten minutes, his mother reminded him, as she did on almost every call, to take care of himself and not to overwork, before hanging up with one last "I love you" that, as always, warmed something deep inside him without his quite knowing how to explain it.

He sat silently on the couch for a moment, the cat now settled on his lap, before dialing a second number. It barely rang twice before a soft, slightly breathless voice answered.

— Hey you, his girlfriend said, a hint of a smile audible in her voice alone. I was just about to call you.

— Oh yeah? said Takeshi, a genuine smile settling on his face for the first time since morning. Serious telepathy between us, then.

— Always, she answered with a soft laugh. Did your day go okay?

— The port, the containers, Marco grumbling about soccer, he summed up with a touch of tired humor. Nothing new under the sun.

— And you, are you okay? Really? she asked after a short silence, her voice becoming more attentive, softer still.

Takeshi hesitated a moment, his gaze drifting toward the window, where night had now fully settled in.

— Yeah, I'm okay, he said finally. I was just a little tired today. Nothing serious.

— Those nightmares you told me about again? she pressed gently, never forcing, simply there.

— A little, he admitted in a low voice. But it's nothing, really. It'll pass.

She didn't answer right away, and he could almost picture her at the other end of the line, choosing her words carefully, the way she always did when it came to him.

— You know you can talk to me about it, if you ever need to, she said softly. I'll always be there to listen.

A short silence settled, warm in spite of everything, before Takeshi answered, his voice a little softer, a little more vulnerable than he would have let it sound in front of anyone else.

— I know. Thanks.

They kept talking for a while, about simple things, everyday things, a movie she wanted to see the following weekend, before finally wishing each other good night, Takeshi's voice a little lighter than at the start of the call. He hung up, set his phone down on the coffee table and stayed still for a moment in the silence of his apartment, the cat still curled up against him, that same dull tiredness still lurking somewhere deep inside him — but a little less heavy, for tonight, thanks to those two voices that, each in its own way, reminded him that he might not be quite as alone as he sometimes liked to believe.

After hanging up, Takeshi stayed on the couch for a while, the cat still snuggled against him, before finally grabbing the remote and turning on the TV almost automatically. He flipped through a few channels without much conviction, finally stopping on some entertainment show whose name or exact subject he couldn't have told you ten minutes later. The low volume, the distant voices and the canned laughter made enough background noise to occupy his mind without demanding any real attention.

The day's fatigue got the better of him faster than he expected. His head slid against the back of the couch, his eyelids grew heavy, and he sank into sleep without even realizing it, the bluish light of the screen still dancing across his relaxed face.

The nightmare came, as always, without warning.

He was in a house he never fully recognized, and yet it always felt familiar to him in a visceral, almost painful way. Flames were already licking the walls around him, a fire whose color was never quite normal — too blue in places, as if the blaze itself refused to obey the ordinary laws of fire. Outside, through a window warped by the heat, he could make out bodies lying on the ground, motionless, in a reddish glow and a muffled roar of screams and metallic noises he never managed to clearly identify.

A hand gripped his, so tightly it hurt, like every time. He looked up at his father, whose face always stayed blurry, ungraspable, like a photograph someone had deliberately smudged. His father leaned toward him, his voice tense, urgent, almost pleading.

— Hide, he said, always the same sentence, the same desperate tone. Whatever happens, don't come out. Don't say anything. Hide.

Then his father straightened up, let go of his hand and walked away toward the door, toward the battlefield you could sense beyond the flames, disappearing into that reddish glow without ever looking back — and Takeshi stayed there, alone, frozen, unable to move, unable to scream, like every time for months now.

He woke with a start, short of breath, his heart pounding violently against his chest, his hands clutching the couch cushions. The TV was still playing its indifferent background noise, the room bathed in a bluish half-light. He stayed still for a moment, trying to calm his breathing, glancing at the oven clock visible from the living room: 3:04 a.m.

The cat was no longer on his lap. He didn't see it anywhere, in fact, which vaguely worried him without his knowing why.

He got up, his throat dry, that familiar post-nightmare unease still weighing on him, and went to the kitchen to pour himself a glass of water. He opened his fridge out of reflex, without really thinking — and stopped dead.

It was empty.

Not just running low, or missing a few things. Empty. Completely empty, as if it had never held anything, the plastic shelves bare and clean, without the slightest trace of food, a bottle, anything at all that should have been there.

Takeshi blinked, closed the door, opened it again — still empty. An icy shiver ran down his spine, and only then did he notice, with an incomprehensible delay, that something much bigger was wrong all around him.

He slowly turned toward the rest of the apartment.

There was nothing left.

No table, no chairs, no shelves, no frames on the walls he knew by heart. The kitchen itself seemed to have been stripped to the bare minimum — a sink, an empty fridge, a bare countertop — and beyond it, in what should have been his living room, there was nothing but his couch, alone, isolated in the middle of a space far too big, far too silent, as if the rest of the apartment had simply stopped existing without his noticing.

Even the TV had disappeared.

His heart began to pound even harder, a cold panic gradually replacing the confusion. He rushed toward the spot where the front door should have been — and froze in front of a wall.

A solid, uniform wall, as if no door had ever existed there. No trace of a frame, no hinges, not the slightest irregularity betraying an opening, recent or old. Just a wall, as smooth and impassive as if it had always been there.

— No way, he whispered, his trembling voice echoing strangely in the too-thick silence. It's a dream. It's just a fucking dream.

He shut his eyes tight, trying to convince himself by sheer willpower that all this was just some weird extension of his usual nightmare, that he would wake up any second in his real bed, or at least on his real couch, surrounded by his real furniture. He pinched his arm, hard enough for the pain to be real, undeniable.

Nothing changed.

He opened his eyes onto the same bare wall, the same empty kitchen, the same oppressive silence. He tried slapping himself lightly, with no more result, his breathing growing more and more ragged as the reality of the situation slowly began to sink in: this wasn't a dream.

Something, tonight, had changed for good — and he had absolutely no idea what it was, or how to get out of it.

The silence that followed this impossible realization didn't last long. A voice suddenly rang out in the empty space, a light voice, almost childlike, but loaded with an intonation that had absolutely nothing innocent about it — a voice that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once, bouncing off walls that shouldn't have produced any echo at all.

— Hello, little toy, we're going to have fun and you're going to play with me..., it said, each word drawn out with an artificial, almost melodious sweetness. And if you don't want to, you'll die, it added, followed by an icy, demonic laugh that seemed to vibrate straight against Takeshi's bones.

He spun around, frantically searching for a silhouette, a source, anything at all to tie that voice to — but there was still only emptiness, the isolated couch, and that impossible wall where his door should have been.

— Who... who's there? he managed to get out, his voice betraying a terror he no longer even tried to hide.

No immediate answer came. A heavy silence settled, a few seconds that felt far longer than they should have, during which he had the unbearable feeling of being watched from every side at once, as if the empty space itself had eyes.

— First, let's take a look at your memories, the voice finally went on, closer now, more intimate, as if it were leaning right up to his ear with no physical presence to be seen.

Takeshi felt something strange and deeply disturbing happening inside his own mind — a sensation of invisible fingers rummaging through his thoughts, his memories, as intrusive as it was impossible to push away. Images flashed by against his will, uncontrollable: the blue fire, his father's hand, years of anonymous orphanages, the faces of tired adults who had never really tried to understand where he came from, the loneliness of a childhood spent never truly belonging anywhere.

He brought his hands to his head, a whimper of mingled pain and fear escaping him, trying in vain to push back this intrusion he could neither see nor fight.

— Stop... stop it, he whispered, his voice broken, his legs threatening to give way beneath him.

After a few seconds that felt like an eternity, the sensation stopped as abruptly as it had started, leaving him gasping, on his knees without even realizing it, his hands still pressed against his temples.

— I see you haven't had a very happy life, the voice went on, an almost joyful enthusiasm piercing through every word, completely disconnected from their meaning. That's wonderful, we're the same, we'll be friends for life.

Takeshi raised his head, short of breath, still desperately searching for a direction, a face, something tangible to hold on to in this oppressive emptiness that stubbornly refused to reveal the slightest physical presence.

— Show yourself, he managed to say, his voice trembling but regaining a scrap of determination, a remnant of survival instinct refusing to just let him collapse. Who are you? What do you want from me?

The laugh rang out again, even closer this time, that same icy, childish sound that seemed to unfold in several directions at once, as if the voice itself refused to be pinned down.

— Oh, but we have all the time in the world for introductions, little toy, it answered, a hint of cruel mischief vibrating beneath the apparent sweetness of its tone. For now... just play with me.

A new cold, deeper, more concrete than anything he had felt so far, suddenly seemed to flood the empty room around him — and Takeshi understood, with a chilling certainty that knotted his stomach, that whatever this invisible presence was, it had absolutely no intention of letting him go before it had gotten, one way or another, what it had come for.

Takeshi stayed huddled for a moment, desperately looking for a way out of this place that no longer existed, out of this voice that seemed to enjoy his terror like a broken toy. An icy dizziness overcame him — the unbearable feeling that he would never get out of this empty space, that this invisible presence would keep going, endlessly, digging through his most painful memories for its own amusement.

He got up with difficulty, legs shaking, and headed for the kitchen, for the drawer where he knew, out of pure habit, he would find a knife. His fingers closed around it, the cold metal a contrast with the feverish heat of his skin.

— Little toy, what are you planning to do with that? the voice rang out, a mocking amusement piercing through an unexpected hint of irritation. That's not very smart, you know.

Takeshi didn't answer. Some part of him, deep down, vaguely understood that if this place wasn't real — if it was a trap, an illusion, anything other than a true physical prison — then maybe the only way out was to refuse to stay, whatever the cost.

— You shouldn't do that, the voice went on, sharper this time, almost an order. I forbid it.

He closed his eyes, his hand shaking violently around the knife handle, the image of his father in the flames, of his mother on the phone, of his girlfriend's gentle face flashing one last time behind his closed eyelids — and in one sudden, desperate motion, more instinct than thought, he pressed the blade into himself.

The pain was immediate, burning, real in a way that contradicted absolutely everything he had hoped for from a mere illusion. A scream escaped him, the little girl's voice letting out a howl of rage somewhere around him, furious, as if someone had just yanked a toy out of her hands too early — and then, nothing.

Total black. Silent. Bottomless.

Takeshi's eyes snapped open, his breath cut short, a strangled cry freezing in his throat.

He was lying on his couch.

The TV was still playing its indifferent background noise, the bluish light dancing on the familiar walls of his living room — his real living room, with his real table, his real shelves, everything perfectly intact, as if nothing had ever happened. The cat, curled up in a ball at the other end of the couch, lifted its head toward him, barely bothered, before going right back to sleep.

He brought a trembling hand to his stomach, to the exact spot where he remembered pressing the blade — nothing. No wound. No trace of blood, no tear in his T-shirt. Nothing to prove that any of it had really happened.

He sat there for a long time, his heart pounding wildly, his ragged breathing struggling to find a normal rhythm, his eyes frantically sweeping every familiar corner of his apartment as if looking for the slightest crack, the slightest sign that this wasn't over, that the voice would ring out again any second.

The oven clock, visible from the couch, read 3:07. Barely three minutes had passed since he last woke up.

Takeshi stayed motionless, the imaginary knife still clenched in a fist that, in reality, was no longer holding anything at all, a chilling certainty slowly settling in him: whatever had just happened, it was neither an ordinary dream nor a simple effect of his fatigue.

And somewhere, lurking in the shadow of his own existence, that thing — that voice, that presence that had called him "little toy" with chilling affection — clearly wasn't done with him.

The days that followed were strange, suspended between two realities Takeshi could no longer clearly tell apart. He had eventually made an appointment with a psychologist, a woman in her forties with a plain, bright office, hoping to find an explanation there, some semblance of logic in what had happened to him. He had told her everything, with almost obsessive precision — the emptiness of his apartment, the wall where his door should have been, the voice, the knife, waking up without a wound.

She had listened carefully, nodded at the right moments, taken regular notes in her notebook — then finally spoke to him, with a well-practiced professional gentleness, about post-traumatic stress, hypnagogic hallucinations, the way a tired mind marked by old trauma could sometimes produce experiences of disturbing intensity, almost indistinguishable from reality.

— What you went through was very real to you, she had said, her tone measured and kind. But that doesn't mean it was real in the physical sense. Your mind went through something very intense.

Takeshi had nodded politely, without ever really believing it. He had tried talking about it with his mother too, then with his girlfriend — each of them reacted with the same affectionate worry, the same sincere desire to reassure him, and the same total inability to imagine that what he was describing could really have happened. No one doubted his suffering. Everyone doubted the nature of what he had lived through.

He had eventually stopped talking about it, keeping to himself that stubborn, almost irrational certainty that something very real had gotten into his apartment that night. It lived in him all the time now, a background hum that never fully left him, not even at work, not even on the phone with the people he loved.

It was while turning over, for perhaps the hundredth time, the confused memories of his childhood that a detail resurfaced — a library, in a small town he had passed through once, years earlier, said to be run by a slightly strange old man, a lover of legends and stories that no one else seemed to know. That memory, as vague and unlikely as it was, forced itself on him with an insistence he couldn't explain, like a thin thread to hold on to.

He took his car one Saturday morning, driving nearly two hours along a country road lined with fields and sparse woods, without even knowing exactly what he hoped to find there.

The library turned out to be an old building, a little sunken in on itself, squeezed between a closed grocery store and a church whose bell tower leaned slightly. He pushed open the heavy wooden door, a discreet chime announcing his entrance into an immediate smell of old paper and dust. The front desk, a simple counter of dark wood, was deserted.

— Is anybody here? he called, his voice echoing strangely in the hushed silence of the place.

No answer came. He waited a moment, then, for lack of anything better, decided to venture alone between the tall, crowded shelves, searching without much method for a section that might match what he was looking for — legends, myths, folklore, anything that might, one way or another, echo what he had been through.

He spent long minutes scanning dusty titles, leafing here and there through books with cracked covers, without ever finding anything that seemed truly relevant. Frustration began to rise in him, mixed with a growing sense of how ridiculous his whole trip was.

— This is completely stupid, he muttered out loud, closing a book with an annoyed snap. I could've searched the internet instead of driving two hours to some middle-of-nowhere library.

— Believe me, you wouldn't have found anything on your phone, young man, said a voice behind him, calm and composed, tinged with slight amusement.

Takeshi jumped violently, spinning around, his heart suddenly beating far too fast for a simple dusty library. An old man stood there, between two shelves, a dark wooden cane in one hand, a leather-bound book in the other, his sharp, piercing gaze strangely at odds with his age-lined features.

The old man took a few steps forward, his cane tapping softly against the old parquet with each movement, an enigmatic smile hovering on his thin lips.

— On the internet you'll never find what's in here, he said, setting his book back on a nearby shelf, his eyes still fixed on Takeshi with an almost unsettling attentiveness. If you're looking for information, I can help you.

Takeshi stayed silent for a moment, hesitating, weighing the pros and cons of confiding in a complete stranger about something even his own family refused to believe. But something in the old man's gaze — a sharpness, a total absence of mocking skepticism — finally pushed him to speak.

— I'm looking for... a creature, he said at last, choosing his words carefully. Something that gets into dreams, or creates them, I'm not really sure. A voice. A presence. It happened to me a few days ago, and I can't find any normal explanation for what I went through.

The old man seemed neither surprised nor skeptical. He nodded slowly, as if that description already matched something very specific in his mind.

— A voice, he repeated thoughtfully, turning toward one of the farthest shelves in the room. Childlike, perhaps? Loaded with a cruelty at odds with its tone?

Takeshi felt a shiver run down his spine.

— Yes, exactly that. How did you...

The old man didn't answer right away, his thin fingers already running along the worn spines of a row of old books, pausing on several titles before dismissing them with an almost imperceptible shake of the head. He finally stopped on a volume thicker than the others, its dark leather binding cracked with time, and gently pulled it from the shelf.

He turned the book toward Takeshi, revealing a title engraved in gold letters, half worn away by the decades:

The Chronicles of Alastor

— It may not be exactly what you're looking for, the old man said, opening the book with an almost reverent delicacy, turning a few yellowed pages covered in tight handwriting and old engravings of distorted silhouettes, smiles too wide to be human. But something tells me the answer you're looking for isn't far from these pages.

Takeshi took the book from the old man's hands with an almost reverent caution, as if the volume itself might, one way or another, be dangerous. He sat down at a small table nearby, under the yellowish light of an old lamp, and began going through the pages the old man had pointed him to, his eyes devouring every line with feverish attention.

The text described Alastor with unsettling precision — his passage into Hell, his meteoric rise among the demons, his role as advisor to a king the book only half named. But it was a passage further along in the chapter that made his heart speed up, his fingers tightening slightly on the fragile edges of the pages.

When Alastor came to Earth, a young child he brought back to life. She fused and became an abominable creature named Poppy, who plays with living creatures and absorbs them after killing them. If one manages to escape the dream, Poppy will try to find you and will kill you without playing with you.

Takeshi reread the passage a second time, then a third, as if repetition would make the words less terrifying than they were. His throat tightened, an icy cold slowly settling into his chest.

— Poppy, he murmured, almost despite himself, the name echoing strangely in the silence of the library.

The old man, who had sat down on a nearby chair without Takeshi really noticing, nodded slowly, his face suddenly graver.

— You've met her, haven't you? he asked; it wasn't really a question.

Takeshi looked up at him, panic beginning to show clearly on his face.

— If this book is telling the truth... I managed to get out. I... I hurt myself to get out of the dream.

The old man stayed silent a moment, his gaze darkening further, before gently closing the book that had stayed open between them on the table.

— Then if this text doesn't lie, he said in a low, steady voice, but charged with a new gravity, that creature won't forget you so easily. She'll look for you. And next time, young man, she won't come to play.

A heavy silence settled between them, broken only by the distant ticking of a clock somewhere at the back of the library, while Takeshi felt, for the first time since that night, the abstract fear inside him turn into something much more concrete, much more urgent: a threat that, from now on, knew exactly where to find him.

The old man slowly rose from his chair, his cane tapping the parquet again as he headed toward another shelf, even farther back than the last, plunged in a gloom the library's dim lighting struggled to reach.

— There may be a way to protect you, he said over his shoulder, his fingers already running along the worn spines of other old volumes. Some texts mention methods, rituals, protections against entities of this kind. But I have to be honest with you, young man.

He turned back to Takeshi, his gaze grave, almost solemn.

— It's unlikely that you can truly escape Poppy once she has set her attention on you. This kind of creature doesn't really know failure. She has that name, that reputation, precisely because she always ends up finding the ones she hunts.

Takeshi felt his stomach knot even tighter, his hands instinctively gripping the edges of the table in front of him.

— So what am I supposed to do? he asked, his voice trembling slightly despite his efforts to keep up some semblance of calm. Wait for her to come and kill me?

The old man didn't answer right away, slowly coming back to the table with several more volumes held against him, which he set down one by one in front of Takeshi with particular care.

— What I can offer you are leads, he said at last. Partial protections, perhaps. Ways to delay the inevitable, to make things harder for her. But I can't promise you a real way out. No one, as far as I know, has ever truly managed to escape this kind of entity once it has decided to "play."

He sat back down across from him, his piercing gaze fixed on Takeshi with a new intensity, as if trying to assess something only he could perceive.

— What I can tell you, however, he added more gently, is that the simple fact that you survived your first encounter with her, by wounding yourself on purpose to escape the dream, is already remarkable in itself. Most people never have that clarity, that composure, in a moment like that. It may not save you for good. But it means you may not be quite the easy prey she expects to find.

Takeshi lowered his eyes to the books piled up in front of him, a host of contradictory feelings jostling inside him — terror, still there, but also a new determination, fragile, only just beginning to take shape.

— Then show me, he said finally, raising his head toward the old man with a firmer gaze than he would have thought possible a few moments earlier. Everything you know. I want to try, even if the odds are slim.

A slight smile, full of both compassion and sincere respect, formed on the old man's lips as he opened the first of the volumes laid out before them.

— Very well, young man, he said softly. Then let's begin at the beginning.

He looked out the hut's small window for a moment, watching the cranes slowly resume their movement in the distance, the hanging containers swaying gently against the gray sky. — You look tired, Sana said suddenly, watching him a little more closely than usual. You okay? Takeshi gave a slight shrug, his eyes still turned toward the window. — Yeah, I'm fine. Just slept badly. — The nightmares again? she asked, more softly this time, without the slightest trace of mockery in her voice. He hesitated a moment before answering, his fingers tightening slightly around the hot cup. — Something like that, yeah. Marco, who had followed the exchange without really wanting to get involved, gently set his mug down on the table. — Maybe you should see someone about that, kid. It's been going on for years, hasn't it? — It's nothing, Takeshi said, a little sharper than he meant to, before catching himself. Really. It always passes after a while. A slightly awkward silence settled for a few seconds, broken only by the crackle of the coffee maker and the dull, distant thud of containers being maneuvered outside. Sana eventually changed the subject, with the quiet tact of someone who knew not to push, and started telling a story about a delivery guy who had nearly dropped an entire crate of electronics the day before. Takeshi listened, nodded at the right moments, let out a polite smile when it was called for — but his mind stayed anchored somewhere else, somewhere between the blurry memory of a blue fire and that dull tiredness that, lately, never seemed to leave him entirely. The siren rang again, shriller this time, signaling the end of the break. Marco got up first, grumbling about how time went by too fast, followed by Sana, who slipped her phone into her pocket before giving Takeshi's shoulder a friendly pat on her way past. — Take care of yourself, okay? she said simply. Takeshi nodded, drained the last mouthfuls of his lukewarm coffee and got up in turn, pulling his gloves back on before pushing the hut door open onto the cold and the fine rain of the quay. The cranes were already resuming their endless ballet above him, and he went back to work without another word, his radio crackling against his shoulder, his thoughts still hooked, despite himself, on that tiredness he simply couldn't explain anymore. Night was already falling when Takeshi left the port, his fluorescent vest swapped for a plain jacket, his hands still a little numb from the cold despite his gloves. He walked to the nearest bus stop, waited about ten minutes under a half-broken shelter, then made the usual trip back to his neighborhood, his head resting against the cold window, watching the city lights roll past without really seeing them. Once home, he took off his shoes, turned on the hallway light and let himself drop onto the couch with a weary sigh. The cat appeared almost immediately, rubbing insistently against his leg, demanding its evening meal. Takeshi got back up, filled its usual bowl, then went back to sit down, his phone in his hand. He called his mother first, bringing the phone to his ear while absently rubbing the back of his neck with his other hand. It rang twice before a warm voice answered at the other end. — Takeshi! How nice, his mother said, a note of happy surprise in her voice. How was your day? — Tiring, as usual, he answered with a slight smile, settling more comfortably against the back of the couch. But I'm fine. What about you, everything okay? — Oh, you know, same as always here, she said. Your father tried to fix the gutter by himself again, I'll let you imagine how that went. Takeshi let out a small laugh, a genuine one this time, a quiet warmth settling in him at the sound of that familiar voice. — He'll never change. — No, never, she agreed with amused tenderness. And you, are you at least eating properly? You're not working too much? — I'm eating fine, Mom, don't worry, he said, his tone a little softer than usual. I've got it handled. They traded a few more bits of unimportant news — the garden, a neighbor, a cousin who had just had a baby — the conversation drifting easily from one topic to the next, as it always did between them. After about ten minutes, his mother reminded him, as she did on almost every call, to take care of himself and not to overwork, before hanging up with one last "I love you" that, as always, warmed something deep inside him without his quite knowing how to explain it. He sat silently on the couch for a moment, the cat now settled on his lap, before dialing a second number. It barely rang twice before a soft, slightly breathless voice answered. — Hey you, his girlfriend said, a hint of a smile audible in her voice alone. I was just about to call you. — Oh yeah? said Takeshi, a genuine smile settling on his face for the first time since morning. Serious telepathy between us, then. — Always, she answered with a soft laugh. Did your day go okay? — The port, the containers, Marco grumbling about soccer, he summed up with a touch of tired humor. Nothing new under the sun. — And you, are you okay? Really? she asked after a short silence, her voice becoming more attentive, softer still. Takeshi hesitated a moment, his gaze drifting toward the window, where night had now fully settled in. — Yeah, I'm okay, he said finally. I was just a little tired today. Nothing serious. — Those nightmares you told me about again? she pressed gently, never forcing, simply there. — A little, he admitted in a low voice. But it's nothing, really. It'll pass. She didn't answer right away, and he could almost picture her at the other end of the line, choosing her words carefully, the way she always did when it came to him. — You know you can talk to me about it, if you ever need to, she said softly. I'll always be there to listen. A short silence settled, warm in spite of everything, before Takeshi answered, his voice a little softer, a little more vulnerable than he would have let it sound in front of anyone else. — I know. Thanks. They kept talking for a while, about simple things, everyday things, a movie she wanted to see the following weekend, before finally wishing each other good night, Takeshi's voice a little lighter than at the start of the call. He hung up, set his phone down on the coffee table and stayed still for a moment in the silence of his apartment, the cat still curled up against him, that same dull tiredness still lurking somewhere deep inside him — but a little less heavy, for tonight, thanks to those two voices that, each in its own way, reminded him that he might not be quite as alone as he sometimes liked to believe. After hanging up, Takeshi stayed on the couch for a while, the cat still snuggled against him, before finally grabbing the remote and turning on the TV almost automatically. He flipped through a few channels without much conviction, finally stopping on some entertainment show whose name or exact subject he couldn't have told you ten minutes later. The low volume, the distant voices and the canned laughter made enough background noise to occupy his mind without demanding any real attention. The day's fatigue got the better of him faster than he expected. His head slid against the back of the couch, his eyelids grew heavy, and he sank into sleep without even realizing it, the bluish light of the screen still dancing across his relaxed face. The nightmare came, as always, without warning. He was in a house he never fully recognized, and yet it always felt familiar to him in a visceral, almost painful way. Flames were already licking the walls around him, a fire whose color was never quite normal — too blue in places, as if the blaze itself refused to obey the ordinary laws of fire. Outside, through a window warped by the heat, he could make out bodies lying on the ground, motionless, in a reddish glow and a muffled roar of screams and metallic noises he never managed to clearly identify. A hand gripped his, so tightly it hurt, like every time. He looked up at his father, whose face always stayed blurry, ungraspable, like a photograph someone had deliberately smudged. His father leaned toward him, his voice tense, urgent, almost pleading. — Hide, he said, always the same sentence, the same desperate tone. Whatever happens, don't come out. Don't say anything. Hide. Then his father straightened up, let go of his hand and walked away toward the door, toward the battlefield you could sense beyond the flames, disappearing into that reddish glow without ever looking back — and Takeshi stayed there, alone, frozen, unable to move, unable to scream, like every time for months now. He woke with a start, short of breath, his heart pounding violently against his chest, his hands clutching the couch cushions. The TV was still playing its indifferent background noise, the room bathed in a bluish half-light. He stayed still for a moment, trying to calm his breathing, glancing at the oven clock visible from the living room: 3:04 a.m. The cat was no longer on his lap. He didn't see it anywhere, in fact, which vaguely worried him without his knowing why. He got up, his throat dry, that familiar post-nightmare unease still weighing on him, and went to the kitchen to pour himself a glass of water. He opened his fridge out of reflex, without really thinking — and stopped dead. It was empty. Not just running low, or missing a few things. Empty. Completely empty, as if it had never held anything, the plastic shelves bare and clean, without the slightest trace of food, a bottle, anything at all that should have been there. Takeshi blinked, closed the door, opened it again — still empty. An icy shiver ran down his spine, and only then did he notice, with an incomprehensible delay, that something much bigger was wrong all around him. He slowly turned toward the rest of the apartment. There was nothing left. No table, no chairs, no shelves, no frames on the walls he knew by heart. The kitchen itself seemed to have been stripped to the bare minimum — a sink, an empty fridge, a bare countertop — and beyond it, in what should have been his living room, there was nothing but his couch, alone, isolated in the middle of a space far too big, far too silent, as if the rest of the apartment had simply stopped existing without his noticing. Even the TV had disappeared. His heart began to pound even harder, a cold panic gradually replacing the confusion. He rushed toward the spot where the front door should have been — and froze in front of a wall. A solid, uniform wall, as if no door had ever existed there. No trace of a frame, no hinges, not the slightest irregularity betraying an opening, recent or old. Just a wall, as smooth and impassive as if it had always been there. — No way, he whispered, his trembling voice echoing strangely in the too-thick silence. It's a dream. It's just a fucking dream. He shut his eyes tight, trying to convince himself by sheer willpower that all this was just some weird extension of his usual nightmare, that he would wake up any second in his real bed, or at least on his real couch, surrounded by his real furniture. He pinched his arm, hard enough for the pain to be real, undeniable. Nothing changed. He opened his eyes onto the same bare wall, the same empty kitchen, the same oppressive silence. He tried slapping himself lightly, with no more result, his breathing growing more and more ragged as the reality of the situation slowly began to sink in: this wasn't a dream. Something, tonight, had changed for good — and he had absolutely no idea what it was, or how to get out of it. The silence that followed this impossible realization didn't last long. A voice suddenly rang out in the empty space, a light voice, almost childlike, but loaded with an intonation that had absolutely nothing innocent about it — a voice that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once, bouncing off walls that shouldn't have produced any echo at all. — Hello, little toy, we're going to have fun and you're going to play with me..., it said, each word drawn out with an artificial, almost melodious sweetness. And if you don't want to, you'll die, it added, followed by an icy, demonic laugh that seemed to vibrate straight against Takeshi's bones. He spun around, frantically searching for a silhouette, a source, anything at all to tie that voice to — but there was still only emptiness, the isolated couch, and that impossible wall where his door should have been. — Who... who's there? he managed to get out, his voice betraying a terror he no longer even tried to hide. No immediate answer came. A heavy silence settled, a few seconds that felt far longer than they should have, during which he had the unbearable feeling of being watched from every side at once, as if the empty space itself had eyes. — First, let's take a look at your memories, the voice finally went on, closer now, more intimate, as if it were leaning right up to his ear with no physical presence to be seen. Takeshi felt something strange and deeply disturbing happening inside his own mind — a sensation of invisible fingers rummaging through his thoughts, his memories, as intrusive as it was impossible to push away. Images flashed by against his will, uncontrollable: the blue fire, his father's hand, years of anonymous orphanages, the faces of tired adults who had never really tried to understand where he came from, the loneliness of a childhood spent never truly belonging anywhere. He brought his hands to his head, a whimper of mingled pain and fear escaping him, trying in vain to push back this intrusion he could neither see nor fight. — Stop... stop it, he whispered, his voice broken, his legs threatening to give way beneath him. After a few seconds that felt like an eternity, the sensation stopped as abruptly as it had started, leaving him gasping, on his knees without even realizing it, his hands still pressed against his temples. — I see you haven't had a very happy life, the voice went on, an almost joyful enthusiasm piercing through every word, completely disconnected from their meaning. That's wonderful, we're the same, we'll be friends for life. Takeshi raised his head, short of breath, still desperately searching for a direction, a face, something tangible to hold on to in this oppressive emptiness that stubbornly refused to reveal the slightest physical presence. — Show yourself, he managed to say, his voice trembling but regaining a scrap of determination, a remnant of survival instinct refusing to just let him collapse. Who are you? What do you want from me? The laugh rang out again, even closer this time, that same icy, childish sound that seemed to unfold in several directions at once, as if the voice itself refused to be pinned down. — Oh, but we have all the time in the world for introductions, little toy, it answered, a hint of cruel mischief vibrating beneath the apparent sweetness of its tone. For now... just play with me. A new cold, deeper, more concrete than anything he had felt so far, suddenly seemed to flood the empty room around him — and Takeshi understood, with a chilling certainty that knotted his stomach, that whatever this invisible presence was, it had absolutely no intention of letting him go before it had gotten, one way or another, what it had come for. Takeshi stayed huddled for a moment, desperately looking for a way out of this place that no longer existed, out of this voice that seemed to enjoy his terror like a broken toy. An icy dizziness overcame him — the unbearable feeling that he would never get out of this empty space, that this invisible presence would keep going, endlessly, digging through his most painful memories for its own amusement. He got up with difficulty, legs shaking, and headed for the kitchen, for the drawer where he knew, out of pure habit, he would find a knife. His fingers closed around it, the cold metal a contrast with the feverish heat of his skin. — Little toy, what are you planning to do with that? the voice rang out, a mocking amusement piercing through an unexpected hint of irritation. That's not very smart, you know. Takeshi didn't answer. Some part of him, deep down, vaguely understood that if this place wasn't real — if it was a trap, an illusion, anything other than a true physical prison — then maybe the only way out was to refuse to stay, whatever the cost. — You shouldn't do that, the voice went on, sharper this time, almost an order. I forbid it. He closed his eyes, his hand shaking violently around the knife handle, the image of his father in the flames, of his mother on the phone, of his girlfriend's gentle face flashing one last time behind his closed eyelids — and in one sudden, desperate motion, more instinct than thought, he pressed the blade into himself. The pain was immediate, burning, real in a way that contradicted absolutely everything he had hoped for from a mere illusion. A scream escaped him, the little girl's voice letting out a howl of rage somewhere around him, furious, as if someone had just yanked a toy out of her hands too early — and then, nothing. Total black. Silent. Bottomless. Takeshi's eyes snapped open, his breath cut short, a strangled cry freezing in his throat. He was lying on his couch. The TV was still playing its indifferent background noise, the bluish light dancing on the familiar walls of his living room — his real living room, with his real table, his real shelves, everything perfectly intact, as if nothing had ever happened. The cat, curled up in a ball at the other end of the couch, lifted its head toward him, barely bothered, before going right back to sleep. He brought a trembling hand to his stomach, to the exact spot where he remembered pressing the blade — nothing. No wound. No trace of blood, no tear in his T-shirt. Nothing to prove that any of it had really happened. He sat there for a long time, his heart pounding wildly, his ragged breathing struggling to find a normal rhythm, his eyes frantically sweeping every familiar corner of his apartment as if looking for the slightest crack, the slightest sign that this wasn't over, that the voice would ring out again any second. The oven clock, visible from the couch, read 3:07. Barely three minutes had passed since he last woke up. Takeshi stayed motionless, the imaginary knife still clenched in a fist that, in reality, was no longer holding anything at all, a chilling certainty slowly settling in him: whatever had just happened, it was neither an ordinary dream nor a simple effect of his fatigue. And somewhere, lurking in the shadow of his own existence, that thing — that voice, that presence that had called him "little toy" with chilling affection — clearly wasn't done with him. The days that followed were strange, suspended between two realities Takeshi could no longer clearly tell apart. He had eventually made an appointment with a psychologist, a woman in her forties with a plain, bright office, hoping to find an explanation there, some semblance of logic in what had happened to him. He had told her everything, with almost obsessive precision — the emptiness of his apartment, the wall where his door should have been, the voice, the knife, waking up without a wound. She had listened carefully, nodded at the right moments, taken regular notes in her notebook — then finally spoke to him, with a well-practiced professional gentleness, about post-traumatic stress, hypnagogic hallucinations, the way a tired mind marked by old trauma could sometimes produce experiences of disturbing intensity, almost indistinguishable from reality. — What you went through was very real to you, she had said, her tone measured and kind. But that doesn't mean it was real in the physical sense. Your mind went through something very intense. Takeshi had nodded politely, without ever really believing it. He had tried talking about it with his mother too, then with his girlfriend — each of them reacted with the same affectionate worry, the same sincere desire to reassure him, and the same total inability to imagine that what he was describing could really have happened. No one doubted his suffering. Everyone doubted the nature of what he had lived through. He had eventually stopped talking about it, keeping to himself that stubborn, almost irrational certainty that something very real had gotten into his apartment that night. It lived in him all the time now, a background hum that never fully left him, not even at work, not even on the phone with the people he loved. It was while turning over, for perhaps the hundredth time, the confused memories of his childhood that a detail resurfaced — a library, in a small town he had passed through once, years earlier, said to be run by a slightly strange old man, a lover of legends and stories that no one else seemed to know. That memory, as vague and unlikely as it was, forced itself on him with an insistence he couldn't explain, like a thin thread to hold on to. He took his car one Saturday morning, driving nearly two hours along a country road lined with fields and sparse woods, without even knowing exactly what he hoped to find there. The library turned out to be an old building, a little sunken in on itself, squeezed between a closed grocery store and a church whose bell tower leaned slightly. He pushed open the heavy wooden door, a discreet chime announcing his entrance into an immediate smell of old paper and dust. The front desk, a simple counter of dark wood, was deserted. — Is anybody here? he called, his voice echoing strangely in the hushed silence of the place. No answer came. He waited a moment, then, for lack of anything better, decided to venture alone between the tall, crowded shelves, searching without much method for a section that might match what he was looking for — legends, myths, folklore, anything that might, one way or another, echo what he had been through. He spent long minutes scanning dusty titles, leafing here and there through books with cracked covers, without ever finding anything that seemed truly relevant. Frustration began to rise in him, mixed with a growing sense of how ridiculous his whole trip was. — This is completely stupid, he muttered out loud, closing a book with an annoyed snap. I could've searched the internet instead of driving two hours to some middle-of-nowhere library. — Believe me, you wouldn't have found anything on your phone, young man, said a voice behind him, calm and composed, tinged with slight amusement. Takeshi jumped violently, spinning around, his heart suddenly beating far too fast for a simple dusty library. An old man stood there, between two shelves, a dark wooden cane in one hand, a leather-bound book in the other, his sharp, piercing gaze strangely at odds with his age-lined features. The old man took a few steps forward, his cane tapping softly against the old parquet with each movement, an enigmatic smile hovering on his thin lips. — On the internet you'll never find what's in here, he said, setting his book back on a nearby shelf, his eyes still fixed on Takeshi with an almost unsettling attentiveness. If you're looking for information, I can help you. Takeshi stayed silent for a moment, hesitating, weighing the pros and cons of confiding in a complete stranger about something even his own family refused to believe. But something in the old man's gaze — a sharpness, a total absence of mocking skepticism — finally pushed him to speak. — I'm looking for... a creature, he said at last, choosing his words carefully. Something that gets into dreams, or creates them, I'm not really sure. A voice. A presence. It happened to me a few days ago, and I can't find any normal explanation for what I went through. The old man seemed neither surprised nor skeptical. He nodded slowly, as if that description already matched something very specific in his mind. — A voice, he repeated thoughtfully, turning toward one of the farthest shelves in the room. Childlike, perhaps? Loaded with a cruelty at odds with its tone? Takeshi felt a shiver run down his spine. — Yes, exactly that. How did you... The old man didn't answer right away, his thin fingers already running along the worn spines of a row of old books, pausing on several titles before dismissing them with an almost imperceptible shake of the head. He finally stopped on a volume thicker than the others, its dark leather binding cracked with time, and gently pulled it from the shelf. He turned the book toward Takeshi, revealing a title engraved in gold letters, half worn away by the decades: The Chronicles of Alastor — It may not be exactly what you're looking for, the old man said, opening the book with an almost reverent delicacy, turning a few yellowed pages covered in tight handwriting and old engravings of distorted silhouettes, smiles too wide to be human. But something tells me the answer you're looking for isn't far from these pages. Takeshi took the book from the old man's hands with an almost reverent caution, as if the volume itself might, one way or another, be dangerous. He sat down at a small table nearby, under the yellowish light of an old lamp, and began going through the pages the old man had pointed him to, his eyes devouring every line with feverish attention. The text described Alastor with unsettling precision — his passage into Hell, his meteoric rise among the demons, his role as advisor to a king the book only half named. But it was a passage further along in the chapter that made his heart speed up, his fingers tightening slightly on the fragile edges of the pages. When Alastor came to Earth, a young child he brought back to life. She fused and became an abominable creature named Poppy, who plays with living creatures and absorbs them after killing them. If one manages to escape the dream, Poppy will try to find you and will kill you without playing with you. Takeshi reread the passage a second time, then a third, as if repetition would make the words less terrifying than they were. His throat tightened, an icy cold slowly settling into his chest. — Poppy, he murmured, almost despite himself, the name echoing strangely in the silence of the library. The old man, who had sat down on a nearby chair without Takeshi really noticing, nodded slowly, his face suddenly graver. — You've met her, haven't you? he asked; it wasn't really a question. Takeshi looked up at him, panic beginning to show clearly on his face. — If this book is telling the truth... I managed to get out. I... I hurt myself to get out of the dream. The old man stayed silent a moment, his gaze darkening further, before gently closing the book that had stayed open between them on the table. — Then if this text doesn't lie, he said in a low, steady voice, but charged with a new gravity, that creature won't forget you so easily. She'll look for you. And next time, young man, she won't come to play. A heavy silence settled between them, broken only by the distant ticking of a clock somewhere at the back of the library, while Takeshi felt, for the first time since that night, the abstract fear inside him turn into something much more concrete, much more urgent: a threat that, from now on, knew exactly where to find him. The old man slowly rose from his chair, his cane tapping the parquet again as he headed toward another shelf, even farther back than the last, plunged in a gloom the library's dim lighting struggled to reach. — There may be a way to protect you, he said over his shoulder, his fingers already running along the worn spines of other old volumes. Some texts mention methods, rituals, protections against entities of this kind. But I have to be honest with you, young man. He turned back to Takeshi, his gaze grave, almost solemn. — It's unlikely that you can truly escape Poppy once she has set her attention on you. This kind of creature doesn't really know failure. She has that name, that reputation, precisely because she always ends up finding the ones she hunts. Takeshi felt his stomach knot even tighter, his hands instinctively gripping the edges of the table in front of him. — So what am I supposed to do? he asked, his voice trembling slightly despite his efforts to keep up some semblance of calm. Wait for her to come and kill me? The old man didn't answer right away, slowly coming back to the table with several more volumes held against him, which he set down one by one in front of Takeshi with particular care. — What I can offer you are leads, he said at last. Partial protections, perhaps. Ways to delay the inevitable, to make things harder for her. But I can't promise you a real way out. No one, as far as I know, has ever truly managed to escape this kind of entity once it has decided to "play." He sat back down across from him, his piercing gaze fixed on Takeshi with a new intensity, as if trying to assess something only he could perceive. — What I can tell you, however, he added more gently, is that the simple fact that you survived your first encounter with her, by wounding yourself on purpose to escape the dream, is already remarkable in itself. Most people never have that clarity, that composure, in a moment like that. It may not save you for good. But it means you may not be quite the easy prey she expects to find. Takeshi lowered his eyes to the books piled up in front of him, a host of contradictory feelings jostling inside him — terror, still there, but also a new determination, fragile, only just beginning to take shape. — Then show me, he said finally, raising his head toward the old man with a firmer gaze than he would have thought possible a few moments earlier. Everything you know. I want to try, even if the odds are slim. A slight smile, full of both compassion and sincere respect, formed on the old man's lips as he opened the first of the volumes laid out before them. — Very well, young man, he said softly. Then let's begin at the beginning.

codex-t1-c10.title: Chapter 10 — Out of Reality's Asshole and a Sunday Dragon Hunt
codex-t1-c10.html:
They retraced their steps across the liquid expanse, Takeshi clutching the crystal sphere against him with an almost pathological caution, every step echoing softly in the heavy silence of the Dimension of Shadows. The portal reappeared on the horizon, exactly where they had left it, a dark tear hanging in the void.

They went through it one by one, the same sensation of total compression passing through them before they reappeared, in a flash of white light, at the center of the metal ring of the Martian base.

Agent 47 was already waiting for them, motionless, as if he hadn't moved a centimeter since they left.

— Two minutes in the real world, he said, his voice as neutral as ever. Interesting. I will pass the information on to the scientists. But first, follow me. Grand Patron Luigi is waiting for you in his office.

He turned on his heel without waiting for an answer, resuming his mechanical walk through the corridors. Takeshi, still a little dazed by the sudden return to reality, exchanged a look with Isidora.

— Two minutes? he repeated. We spent like... an hour in there, didn't we?

— Time doesn't work the same in that kind of place, Isidora answered with a shrug, as if the remark were completely obvious. Don't worry, you'll get used to it.

Lucifer, walking behind them, glanced at the sphere still clutched in Takeshi's hands.

— Be careful with that, he said. I really don't want us to accidentally release the worst god killer of all time in a corridor of Grand Patron Luigi's Martian base.

— Believe me, Takeshi answered, his voice tense, I'm not taking my eyes off it for a second.

They followed Agent 47 through several more corridors, gradually climbing back up to the upper levels of the base, until they reached a door more imposing than the others, guarded by two soldiers who stepped aside instantly as 47 approached.

— The Boss is inside, he said simply, stopping in front of the door. Go in.

Isidora pushed the door open without the slightest hesitation, walking in as if the office already belonged to her. Grand Patron Luigi, for his part, was lounging in a jacuzzi installed right in the room, the bubbling water swirling gently around him — still wearing a full suit, his red tie floating slightly on the surface.

— Bathing suit, you like it? he said with a satisfied smirk, spreading his arms as if to present his outfit.

— You're the one who lives like that, huh, not us, Isidora answered, settling right down on the edge of the jacuzzi without caring in the slightest about how incongruous the scene was.

Takeshi, hanging back with the sphere still clutched in his hands, watched the scene with growing disbelief. After everything he had just been through — Hell, the Dimension of Shadows, an omniscient entity stuck in a chair — seeing the most dangerous man in the known universe splashing around in a jacuzzi in a three-piece suit seemed almost trivial in comparison.

— So, said Grand Patron Luigi, his eyes settling on the crystal sphere, you found your thing?

— Yeah, Lucifer answered, stepping closer in turn, we even got a bonus. The kid's father is alive. Locked up by the Cult of KJ.

Grand Patron Luigi's smile wavered slightly at the mention of KJ, a more calculating gleam crossing his eyes, before he immediately went back to his casual air.

— The Cult, huh, he said. Interesting. Well, anyway, congratulations, kids. You survived a round trip into a dimension that even I considered a gamble.

He sat up slightly in the water, his eyes settling directly on Takeshi, a salesman's smile returning to his face.

— And you, kid, he said, looks like you've got a tough decision to make now. Free a god killer, or go save your father stashed away with KJ's lunatics. Honestly, I wouldn't want to be in your shoes.

Takeshi tightened his grip on the sphere, a semblance of determination finally breaking through the exhaustion and confusion piled up since the start of this impossible day.

— I'm going to free 81 first, he said. And since I'm the one who freed him, maybe he'll help me free my father.

Grand Patron Luigi stayed silent for a moment, his fingers lightly tapping the surface of the water, before an approving smile formed on his face.

— Smart choice, he said. It's true that, from what I know, 81 only hates gods. You're not one. And on top of that, you helped free him. That should be enough for him to owe you at least that much.

Isidora, sitting on the edge of the jacuzzi, raised an eyebrow, a crooked smile stretching across her lips.

— "Should" being the key word in that sentence, huh, she said. We're still talking about a guy who devoured a billion years of deities. Gratitude might not be his strong suit.

— It's a risk worth taking, Takeshi answered, his voice firmer than he would have thought possible a few moments earlier. But between waiting indefinitely to find a way into the Cult of KJ and potentially having the help of the most powerful being in the universe... I'd rather take my chances with him.

Lucifer crossed his arms, watching Takeshi with a new, almost surprised respect.

— Well, well, he said. You might not have much in the way of powers, kid, but you've got balls. Gotta give you that much.

Alastor, who had stayed silent until then, let out a satisfied little laugh.

— Right, he said, so how do we wake him up without him killing all of us the very next second?

Lucifer shrugged, a half-reassuring, half-amused smile hovering on his lips.

— Sure, 81 is a powerful being, he said, but he puts up with Isidora, he's buddies with me, and on top of that we've got the equivalent of KJ in power right here, in a jacuzzi. Should be fine.

Grand Patron Luigi let out a short laugh from his bath, waving a hand through the water with almost royal nonchalance.

— It's sweet of you to count on me as a safety net, he said, but I'm warning you right now: if 81 loses it, I'm not stepping in for free either.

— Of course, Isidora muttered, rolling her eyes. Everything has a price with you.

— Always, Grand Patron Luigi confirmed with a wink.

Takeshi, still a little tense at the idea of releasing an entity capable, in Alastor's own words, of surpassing the Incarnation of Death herself, tightened his grip on the sphere.

— So, he said, if I sum up: we're assuming that if things go wrong, you'll all be there to stop me from getting killed in the next second.

— That's more or less the idea, yes, Lucifer confirmed with a smile.

— Reassuring, Takeshi muttered.

— It's already more than you had when you summoned Alastor all alone in a forest, Alastor pointed out with a wink. At least here, you've got company.

Isidora got up from the edge of the jacuzzi, stretching, her gaze passing over each member of the group with a new energy.

— Okay, she said, so where do we do this? Because I don't really feel like accidentally breaking this sphere in the middle of Grand Patron Luigi's office.

— That's indeed a good question, said Lucifer, and one I'd also rather we answered before doing anything.

Grand Patron Luigi waved a hand through the water, brushing the question aside with a casual gesture.

— Nah, I don't care, he said. You can do it in my office.

A stunned silence greeted this statement, every eye turning to him.

— Wait, said Lucifer, we're talking about freeing 81 here. THE 81. Here, in your office, while you're splashing around in a jacuzzi?

— Yeah, Grand Patron Luigi confirmed with a shrug, as if the remark made absolutely no sense. This room is armored against pretty much everything that exists. If it goes wrong, the damage won't leave this room. And if not, well, too bad for the furniture.

Isidora gave a delighted smile, settling comfortably against the edge of the desk, as if the prospect particularly amused her.

— I like this plan, she said. Honestly, seeing 81 wake up next to a jacuzzi and a guy in a soaking-wet suit has pretty high comedic potential.

Alastor raised an eyebrow, a crooked smile appearing on his face.

— True, it wouldn't be the worst entrance for an entity that's supposed to be terrifying, he said.

Takeshi, for his part, felt his heart beat harder and harder, the sphere still clutched in his hands, the reality of what he was about to do gradually sinking in with a gravity that no offhand remark really managed to lighten.

— Okay, he said finally, his voice trembling slightly. So I... I just throw it on the floor, is that it?

— That's it, Grand Patron Luigi confirmed, sitting up slightly in the jacuzzi, a glint of genuine interest crossing his eyes for the first time. Go ahead, kid. Smash it.

Takeshi took a deep breath, his fingers tightening one last time around the sphere before he raised it above his head and hurled it against the floor with all his strength.

The glass shattered with a sharp crack, almost disappointing in its simplicity, a dust of crystal scattering in a fine cloud that slowly settled onto the office floor.

Then the air tore apart.

A gigantic mass emerged from nothingness in a fraction of a second, a colossus nearly three meters tall, every muscle in his body taut like living stone, two massive swords crossed on his back, their blades seeming to absorb the surrounding light rather than reflect it. His face bore the scars of a billion years of combat — one eye missing, replaced by a deep scar running across his whole face, and countless other marks weathered into his skin, each one telling a story of violence no one in the room could have imagined.

A deathly silence fell over the office, only the faint lapping of the jacuzzi absurdly continuing to disturb the surrounding calm.

81 stood motionless for a moment, his single eye slowly sweeping the room — the jacuzzi, Grand Patron Luigi still soaking in his suit, Lucifer, Alastor, Isidora, and finally Takeshi, still frozen in front of him, his hands empty now that the sphere was nothing but a pile of debris at his feet.

Then, in a deep, hoarse voice, as if rusted by an eternity of forced silence, he finally spoke his first words since being sealed.

— Who... freed me?

Isidora, still leaning nonchalantly against the wall, crossed her arms with a mocking smile.

— Welcome back to the land of the living, she said. Did you miss me?

— I've just come out of a prison where I was locked up for thousands of years, and you ask me that, you big fat bitch! 81 roared, his voice echoing against the office walls with a power that made the windows rattle.

— Calm down, said Lucifer, raising his hands in a soothing gesture. She was useful, after all. Apart from shattering my self-confidence.

81 slowly turned his single eye toward Lucifer, a glint of recognition briefly crossing his scarred face.

— Lucifer, he said, less hostile but still wary. Still alive too, I see.

— We do what we can, Lucifer answered with a cautious smile.

The colossus swept the room with his gaze again, this time stopping on Grand Patron Luigi, still submerged in his jacuzzi, completely unfazed by the situation.

— And who's this, the jackass in the soaking-wet suit? asked 81, one eyebrow — well, the brow ridge above his remaining eye — rising with a mixture of confusion and contempt.

— Grand Patron Luigi, the man himself answered with a salesman's smile, waving a dripping hand in greeting. Pleased to meet you. This is my place, by the way.

81 stared at him for a moment, as if assessing the potential threat, before shrugging slightly, apparently unimpressed.

— Never heard of you, he said.

— You will, Grand Patron Luigi answered without losing his smile.

81's gaze finally settled on Takeshi, who had stayed silent since the colossus woke up, his single eye studying him with an intensity that made the young man take an instinctive step back.

— You, said 81 in a lower, almost calculating voice. You're the one who broke the sphere.

Takeshi straightened up slightly, gathering what little courage he had left.

— Yes, he answered, it was me.

81 stared at him a moment longer, something almost like consideration crossing his weathered face.

— Well, I thank you, demon — even if you've still got more of a human side, he said. You freed me, and that, I won't forget. But first, I have to go kill Rex Stella and all the other bastards who locked me up.

A tense silence settled, Isidora suddenly sitting up straight, her offhand air giving way to sincere worry.

— Wait, wait, she said. We knew you'd want revenge, but right now, straight away? We've barely gotten you out of there.

— I've waited thousands of years, 81 answered, his voice hardening. I'm not waiting one more second.

Takeshi, sensing that this moment might be his only chance, stepped forward, his voice hesitant but determined.

— Wait, he said. Before you go off to kill anyone, I need your help. Well, so to speak. I just freed you, so I was hoping that... maybe... you could help me in return.

81 slowly turned his single eye toward him, a heavy silence settling as he assessed him again, this time with more calculating attention.

— Help you with what, exactly? he asked, a hint of suspicion in his hoarse voice.

— My father, said Takeshi. He's being held by the Cult of KJ. For years now. And I... I can't go there alone.

A silence settled, 81 remaining motionless, his eyes still fixed on Takeshi, as if literally weighing the value of this request against his thirst for immediate revenge.

81 slowly crossed his massive arms, his single eye not leaving Takeshi, a decision visibly forming behind his hard expression.

— Since you freed me, I accept, he said at last. But first, I want my revenge. I promise I'll go take on this unknown cult you're talking about. After.

Takeshi hesitated, a hint of frustration showing through his relief.

— How long will that take? he asked. My revenge, it... well, my father, he's been waiting for years. I wouldn't want it to drag on even longer.

— Depends how long they take to die, 81 answered with chilling calm. Rex Stella and the others locked me up for millennia. I don't intend to do things halfway.

Isidora let out a low whistle, exchanging a look with Lucifer.

— This should be fun, she said.

Grand Patron Luigi, still in his jacuzzi, raised a hand, an amused smile on his lips.

— Mind you, he said, if you want a hand speeding things up, I've got resources. Lots of resources. It could considerably shorten the revenge schedule.

81 turned his gaze toward him, a glint of new interest crossing his scarred face.

— You said you'd never heard of me, he said. So why would you help me?

— Because I like watching chaos get organized efficiently, Grand Patron Luigi answered with a wink. And incidentally, because having a god killer who owes me a favor could come in handy later.

81 let out a deep laugh, almost a rumble, slowly shaking his head.

— You, he said, I'm starting to like you.

Grand Patron Luigi tapped the edge of his jacuzzi, addressing an invisible point on the ceiling.

— Riper, call 47 and tell him to come now. He's going to go with our newly released friend.

A cold, mechanical voice immediately rang out from a speaker hidden somewhere in the room.

— Copy that, Boss. Agent 47 on his way.

Isidora raised an eyebrow, turning to Grand Patron Luigi with amused curiosity.

— Riper? she repeated. What's that, your invisible butler?

— Reaper, Grand Patron Luigi corrected with a patient smile. My AI. Unhackable, always listening, always efficient. Unlike some, he added with a pointed look at Lucifer, who still has breakable wooden doors in his palace.

— Okay, we get it, Lucifer muttered.

A few moments later, the office door opened without the slightest sound, revealing Agent 47, impeccable as ever in his black suit, his eyes sweeping the room with absolute calm — even in the face of the massive and clearly hostile presence of 81, who was already sizing him up with a mixture of curiosity and contempt.

— You called me, Boss, said 47, his voice as neutral as always.

— Yeah, Grand Patron Luigi confirmed. You're going with our friend here, the big one-eyed bruiser, on his little personal revenge trip. Consider it a paid vacation.

47 turned his head toward 81, assessing him in silence for a long moment, not a trace of worry breaking through his usual mask of indifference.

— Understood, he said simply.

81, for his part, let out a deep little laugh, almost amused by the perfect calm of the man facing him.

— You're not scared of me, he said, one eyebrow raised.

— Fear is not one of my parameters, 47 answered without the slightest hesitation.

A silence followed, 81 seeming to weigh that answer with a new interest, almost respect.

— I like this guy, he said finally, turning to Grand Patron Luigi. He's coming with me.

Lucifer turned to Alastor, his tone taking on an unusual seriousness.

— I'm going to follow 81, he said. You, go back to Hell, guard the kingdom for me.

Alastor nodded, a crooked smile reappearing despite the gravity of the moment.

— Count on me, Lulu, he said. I'll try not to break too much while you're away. Well, okay, a little.
